description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes de la preparatoria Hybridge interesados en la programación, la tecnología y la exploración espacial. En este hackathon trabajaremos en el desafío “Abandonados pero no olvidados”, buscando acercar a los jóvenes a la historia de los equipos de la NASA. Nos caracterizan la colaboración y las ganas de aprender. Valoramos habilidades de investigación, diseño, programación y redacción.
summary:
We developed Abandonados, pero no olvidados (“Abandoned, but not Forgotten”), an interactive, Spanish-language web experience that tells the stories of NASA hardware left on Mars and in deep space through the eyes of Roverchito, a curious young robot searching for his origins. Visitors join him on a mission map with five stops: Sojourner and Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Kepler/K2 and Pioneer 10. Each stop combines cinematic scenes where the spacecraft “speak” and share their memories, minigames inspired by real events, and narration by Roverchito’s voice. So far, Spirit’s descent and landing is playable. Every fact comes from NASA sources, which are cited on each page, and the story clearly separates real history from fiction. At the end, Roverchito discovers he was built from the lessons each mission left behind.

This approach turns data about retired equipment into a story school-age audiences can feel, not just read. It shows that a mission’s end is not its end: its discoveries keep shaping exploration. Built by high school students for students, it brings NASA’s legacy to Spanish-speaking young explorers.
details:
What it does and how it works
Abandonados, pero no olvidados is a story-driven web experience in Spanish. It opens with a short cinematic that the visitor starts when ready: Roverchito, a young robot still in development, discovers his origin file is restricted, and Mission Control sends him to visit NASA spacecraft that may know where he comes from.

The journey continues on a mission map with five stops, ordered from Mars outward: Sojourner and Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Kepler/K2 and Pioneer 10. Each stop follows the same structure: an opening cinematic, a minigame based on a real event, and a closing cinematic. In the cinematics, the spacecraft “speak,” share their memories and give Roverchito one note of a melody.

The Spirit stop is fully playable: players make mission decisions, and Roverchito reacts with different expressions. They also land the rover by timing the parachute, airbags and retrorockets. Opportunity and Pioneer 10 already have their cinematics, and Pioneer 10’s ending reveals the full story. When the melody is complete, Roverchito learns that each note is a spacecraft’s last signal, and that he was built from the lessons every mission left behind.

Benefits

  • Free and easy to use: it runs in any browser, with no installation, on computers and phones.
  • Fact-based: every fact comes from our team’s research cards, built from NASA sources. Each stop includes a “Real history” section with links, and fiction is kept separate from facts.
  • Accessible: it works with the keyboard and screen readers, respects reduced-motion settings, and Roverchito’s narration can be muted.

Intended impact
We want middle and high school students, especially Spanish speakers, to care about missions that ended. Students should leave knowing what each spacecraft discovered and understanding that a mission’s end is not its end, because its data keeps shaping exploration. Teachers can also use it in class as an engaging introduction to Mars and deep-space exploration.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks.
  • SVG illustrations: Roverchito was drawn by our team and vectorized, and each spacecraft has its own drawing.
  • Web Speech API for Roverchito’s voice, with support for pre-recorded audio.
  • Web Audio API for the melody.
  • localStorage to save progress.
  • Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages for version control and hosting.
  • Google Docs for research.
  • A Python helper script to manage voice lines.
  • AI-assisted development with Claude Code.
  • NASA imagery used with credit.

Creativity

  • The spacecraft are characters with personalities: Opportunity is a proud, joking twin, and Pioneer 10 is a wise “great-grandfather.”
  • A melody made of last signals connects every stop.
  • Scenes include animated memory scans, flashbacks and voice narration.
  • Minigames recreate real engineering moments.
  • The ending turns facts into a personal discovery for Roverchito.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy: only data from NASA-based research, with sources cited.
  • Age and attention span: short scenes, humor and dialogue instead of lectures.
  • Accessibility and performance, especially on phones.
  • Copyright: credited NASA images and original illustrations.
  • Time constraints: we chose 5 of our 10 researched spacecraft and built a reusable cinematic engine so new stops are faster to add.
  • Teamwork: research cards and stories written by different team members.
